definition.text: The science that studies how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across whole landscapes, and how to improve those relationships.

facts.text: Its hallmark is a focus on how pattern, process and scale relate, and on broad-scale environmental problems.
Landscapes are mixed areas made of interacting patches, from forests and lakes to farms and cities.
Unlike traditional ecology, which often assumes places are uniform, landscape ecology studies spatial patterns and heterogeneity, the way parts of a landscape differ.
German geographer Carl Troll coined the term in 1939 while using aerial photographs to study how environment and vegetation interact.
Its four main principles concern how spatial heterogeneity develops, how things move across it, how it affects living and non-living processes, and how to manage it.
The field treats humans explicitly as a force that changes landscapes and proposes ways to restore degraded ones.
Its recent growth owes much to geographic information systems and large remotely sensed habitat datasets.
By 1980 it was an established discipline, having grown from European planning of human-dominated landscapes.

definition.text: A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings; patches, corridors and the background matrix together make up a landscape's mosaic.

facts.text: The matrix is the well-connected background ecological system of a landscape.
Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is; a forest with fewer open gaps has higher connectivity.
Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides.
Patches change and fluctuate over time, a process called patch dynamics.

definition.text: An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecological communities meet, such as forest giving way to grassland.

facts.text: An edge is the part of an ecosystem near its border, where neighbouring patches make conditions differ from the interior, often changing which species live there.
Ecotones can be natural, like a lakeshore, or made by people, like a field cleared from forest.
An ecotone keeps traits of both neighbouring communities and often holds species found in neither.
Fencerows, forest-to-marsh transitions and riparian zones are classic examples.

definition.text: The breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller separate pieces.

facts.text: Repeated random clearing, natural or human, can break continuous cover into isolated patches.
Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from a connected to a disconnected phase.
Metapopulation models gave conservation biologists a tool to judge how fragmentation affects whether populations survive.

title: Natural Capital Project

definition.text: A research partnership, now called the Natural Capital Alliance, that pushes for more investment in nature by mapping, modelling and valuing its benefits for decision-makers.

facts.text: Gretchen Daily of Stanford founded it in 2005 with The Nature Conservancy and World Wildlife Fund.
It built InVEST, free open-source software with 20+ ecosystem service models, used in more than 185 countries.
Not everyone agrees with its method of putting a money value on nature.

notes: Single organization (NGO partnership); excluded per brief. Its substance is carried by the InVEST model entry.

definition.text: A GIS is a combination of computer hardware and software that stores, manages, analyses, edits and displays geographic data.

facts.text: A GIS uses location as the key that links otherwise unrelated pieces of information, much as a database links tables by a shared key.
Its core is a database holding the shape and position of geographic things along with their attributes.
Roger Tomlinson coined the phrase in the mid-1960s, though many of the methods GIS automates are much older.
Data enter a GIS by direct field measurement such as remote sensing or GPS, by digitizing paper maps, or by copying existing GIS data.
Feeding satellite data into a GIS lets researchers track changes in Earth's surface over days, months and years.
GIS is a commonly used tool for environmental management, modelling and planning, and for monitoring forest cover and deforestation.

definition.text: The two traditional ways a GIS stores geographic data: as raster images made of cells, or as vector points, lines and polygons.

facts.text: Mapped things are usually treated either as discrete objects, like a house or road, or as continuous fields, like rainfall or population density.
A GIS can convert between formats, for example tracing lines around same-class cells of a satellite image to make vector shapes.
Point clouds are a newer hybrid that pair three-dimensional points with colour values.

definition.text: Combining several spatial datasets of the same area into a new one, like stacking maps of one region on top of each other.

facts.text: Overlays work like Venn diagrams: a union keeps everything from both inputs, an intersect keeps only where they overlap.
With rasters, overlay is done by map algebra, a function that combines each layer's cell values and can weight some inputs more than others.
Cartographic modeling, a term Dana Tomlin coined in 1983, means producing and analysing several thematic layers of the same area.

definition.text: Building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between a set of measured sample points.

facts.text: Geostatistics, the branch of statistics for continuous spatial data, models spatial correlation to predict values at unmeasured places.
It is justified by spatial autocorrelation: measurements at one place closely resemble those nearby.
Methods include inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines, Thiessen polygons and trend surfaces.

definition.text: Using GIS to compare alternative places, such as candidate habitat for restoration, against several criteria at once.

facts.text: Decision rules combine the criteria so the alternatives can be ranked or prioritised.
It may cut the cost and time of finding potential restoration sites.

definition.text: The physical material at Earth's land surface, such as plants, concrete, buildings, bare ground or water.

facts.text: Land cover differs from land use, which describes how people use the land and what economic activity happens there, though the terms are often confused.
It is captured mainly by field survey or by analysing remotely sensed images.
Surveys define similar categories differently; there are many definitions of forest, sometimes within one organisation.
FAO statistics put tree-covered areas at 4,335.00 million ha in 2015, 29.11% of land, down 99.93 million ha since 1992.
In FAO data, artificial surfaces grew from 26.04 million ha in 1992 to 55.40 million ha in 2015.
Detecting land cover change gives baseline information for judging climate change impacts on habitats, biodiversity and resources.
Human activity is the biggest cause of land cover change, with deforestation historically a primary driver.

definition.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it, usually by observing Earth from satellites or aircraft.

facts.text: It produces the satellite views in online maps and the cloud pictures in weather forecasts.
It reaches dangerous or remote places and can replace slower, costlier fieldwork without disturbing the site.
Brazil's space research institute has measured Amazon deforestation every year since 1988 using Landsat-class imagery.
Uses include natural resource management, mapping wildlife habitat, greenhouse gas monitoring and oil spill detection.
It can assess the health and extent of land cover that provides ecosystem services, aiding planning and monitoring.
Multispectral satellites such as Landsat have been in use since the early 1970s; satellite remote sensing began with Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Many parts of the water balance, such as soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration and snow, can be measured remotely.

definition.text: The two classes of remote sensing: passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, while active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back.

facts.text: Passive sensors most often measure reflected sunlight; cameras, radiometers and spectrometers are common examples.
Radar and lidar are active systems that time a pulse's return to find the distance to a target.

definition.text: The quality of remote sensing data, described by its spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolution.

facts.text: Spatial resolution is pixel size, typically squares from 1 to 1,000 metres on a side.
Radiometric resolution is how many intensity levels a sensor distinguishes, typically 8 to 14 bits, or 256 up to 16,384 shades per band.
Temporal resolution is how often a satellite or plane passes over, which matters for time series such as deforestation monitoring.
The Hyperion sensor resolves 220 bands from 0.4 to 2.5 μm, while Landsat records seven.

title: False-color composite
article: Remote sensing#False Color Composites (FCCs) and Pseudocolor

definition.text: An image in which wavelengths are assigned to display colours other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see.

facts.text: It is made by changing which parts of the spectrum are shown as red, green and blue.
Pseudocolor instead maps a single band onto a new colour scale; this also works for temperature or elevation.

definition.text: A computer model that simulates the actions and interactions of autonomous agents, such as individuals or organisations, to understand how a whole system behaves.

facts.text: In ecology it is also called an individual-based model.
Its three central ideas are agents as objects, emergence and complexity: simple rules for agents can produce complex behaviour.
Thomas Schelling's 1971 segregation model, done with coins and graph paper, was an early example of agents producing an emergent outcome.
The idea dates to the late 1940s but spread only in the 1990s because it needs heavy computing.
In economics, ABMs drop the assumption of equilibrium and replace representative agents with diverse, interdependent ones, so they can produce booms and crashes.
Combined with GIS, the ABM models the process while the GIS models the spatial pattern.
ABMs are used in water resources planning to test infrastructure and policy and to value cooperation.
Validation checks that a model relates to the real world, through calibration, sensitivity analysis and statistical tests.

definition.text: A probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on one another as a diagram of arrows with no loops.

facts.text: Each node is a variable and each arrow a direct dependency; each node has a probability function based on its parent nodes.
Given an observed event, it can estimate how likely each possible cause was, as with symptoms and diseases.
It automatically applies Bayes' theorem to complex problems, updating beliefs about unobserved variables as evidence comes in.
Bayesian belief networks have been used to explore where ecological regime shifts are likely to happen.

definition.text: An abstract, usually mathematical, representation of an ecological system, from one population to a whole biome, studied to understand the real system.

facts.text: Relationships measured in the field, such as sunlight and water against photosynthesis, are combined into a model that predicts how the real system behaves.
Models allow experiments too costly or unethical to run on real ecosystems, and can simulate centuries in minutes.
There are two main types: simple analytic models solved by equations, and simulation models solved numerically, which are more widely used and more realistic.
Because ecosystems are so complex, models reduce them to a few state variables and group similar species into functional groups.
Spatially explicit, or landscape, models include a varied spatial environment because place can change outcomes greatly.
Models are validated against independent data sets or field observations, with an acceptable gap often set beforehand.
Gaps between a model and observations often suggest new hypotheses about unknown ecological relations.
Ecopath, a simulation system for marine ecosystems, is widely used by fisheries scientists.

title: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model

definition.text: One of the earliest ecological models: a pair of equations, one for a prey species and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together.

facts.text: It was developed by Alfred Lotka in 1925 and Vito Volterra in 1926.
Volterra built it to explain swings in Adriatic fish and shark numbers after fishing was cut back in the First World War.
Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate.
Supporters of the ratio-dependent Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the data are so far from Lotka–Volterra that it can be discounted as wrong.

contested_note: Proponents of the ratio-dependent Arditi–Ginzburg model argue field data reject the Lotka–Volterra form.

title: i-Tree

definition.text: A suite of US Forest Service software tools that measure and value the ecosystem services trees provide in cities and the countryside.

facts.text: It quantifies services such as pollution removal, carbon sequestration and avoided stormwater runoff.
Some tools work bottom-up from ground tree inventories, others top-down from remote sensing data.
Urban foresters use it to assess an urban forest's structure and turn that into ecosystem services and economic value.
It began in 2002 as a sample survey that simulated a full urban tree inventory.

notes: A US government software product; kept because it is a chapter seed with its own article and a standard ecosystem service valuation tool.

definition.text: Land change models describe, project and explain how land use and land cover change over time.

facts.text: They help explain how people have changed and will change Earth's surface, and guide resource decisions from a single plot to whole regions.
Land change modeling is an application of landscape ecology and a key part of land change science, used to assess long-term outcomes for land cover and climate.
Approaches include machine-learning models trained on past land cover, cellular models that compare neighbouring areas, economic supply-and-demand models, agent-based models and hybrids.
A 2011 study in western Mexico found two outwardly similar models gave considerably different results.
All land change models carry irreducible uncertainty, and the further into the future they project, the more uncertain they become.
The model should fit the goal: agent-based models for questions about policy and actors, machine learning and cellular models for spotting patterns and trends.
Practitioners use them to explore the future effects of policies and set guidelines, on topics from water and food to urbanization.
They predict how land may change under different circumstances, which helps risk assessment and policy, with some uncertainty.

definition.text: Checking a land change model by comparing its processes or its predicted maps with what really happened.

facts.text: Pattern validation often uses three maps, the real maps at two dates and the simulated second map, sorting pixels into hits, misses, false alarms and similar classes.
The Figure of Merit turns hits, misses and false alarms into one percentage for the overlap between real and simulated change.
Using data from after the first time period to calibrate can make a model look far more accurate than it really is.

definition.text: A way of measuring distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return.

facts.text: It is an active sensor that supplies its own light and uses the speed of light to turn return time into distance.
From an aircraft it can map terrain at 30-centimetre resolution or better.
In forestry it measures tree heights and crown widths and estimates canopy volume, biomass and carbon density.
A 2024 lidar study found England has 390,000 km of hedgerows.

definition.text: NDVI is a widely used number, calculated from red and near-infrared sensor readings, that measures how dense and healthy vegetation is.

facts.text: Green plants absorb visible light for photosynthesis but strongly reflect near-infrared light, so they look dark in red and bright in near-infrared.
NDVI ranges from -1 to 1: near zero means little vegetation, negative values mean water or non-land, and high values mean dense healthy plants.
Dense canopies tend to give values of about 0.3 to 0.8, while bare soils give small positive values around 0.1 to 0.2.
Researchers studying Great Plains rangeland developed it to correct for the changing sun angle; its earliest reported use was in 1973 by Rouse and colleagues.
It remains the best-known index for detecting live green plant canopies in multispectral data.
Farmers use it to assess crop health, spot plant stress before it is visible and predict yields.
Falling NDVI can signal drought stress, deforestation or land degradation.
NDVI carries only part of the original spectral information and is affected by the atmosphere, sensor differences, soil and snow.

title: Participatory GIS

definition.text: A participatory approach to spatial planning that puts mapping tools in the hands of local people so their own knowledge shapes decisions.

facts.text: It combines sketch maps, 3D models, aerial photos, satellite images and GPS to turn people's spatial knowledge into maps for discussion and decisions.
Its aim is to empower marginalized groups and protect traditional knowledge by leaving control of sensitive maps with those who made them.
Uses range from neighbourhood planning to environmental and natural resource management.
Top-down and bottom-up approaches are the currently debated split, and critics ask who really gets access to the technology.

contested_note: Top-down and bottom-up approaches to participatory GIS are a debated split, with questions over who actually benefits.

title: Runoff curve number

definition.text: An empirical number used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in.

facts.text: The USDA Soil Conservation Service, now the Natural Resources Conservation Service, developed it from runoff measured on small catchments and plots.
It depends on soil group, land use and treatment, and ranges from 30 to 100, with higher numbers meaning more runoff and less permeable ground.
Soils fall into four hydrologic groups, from A, deep sands with high infiltration, to D, clays and shallow soils with very slow infiltration.
Paved parking lots and roofs have a curve number of 98, while open space in good condition on group A soil has 39.

notes: Initial abstraction ratio: traditionally Ia=0.2S, but model fitting (S:5319d25ee91c, S:a4d866f4edbe) suggests 0.05 is more appropriate; a revision rather than a same-definition conflict.

definition.text: A strategic planning method in which organizations imagine several plausible futures in order to make flexible long-term plans.

facts.text: Scenario analysis presents several alternative futures and the paths to them rather than one exact forecast.
Unlike a forecast, it does not just extend past trends or assume past observations will stay valid.
It draws on systems thinking: many factors can combine through feedback loops to create surprising futures.
Analysts choose scenarios that are both possible and uncomfortable, helping decision-makers anticipate change and build more robust strategies.
Most authors credit Herman Kahn, working at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s, with introducing it; Gaston Berger developed similar methods in France.
Royal Dutch Shell adopted it after energy companies lost billions in the 1970s, surprised by environmentalism and the OPEC cartel.
In business, attention has shifted from opponents' behaviour toward changes in the natural environment.

definition.text: The set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics.

facts.text: In a narrower sense it is geospatial analysis, applying statistics and other analysis to data with a geographic aspect, usually with GIS software.
GIS-based spatial analysis was developed for ecology, geology and epidemiology and now reaches natural resources, disaster risk and climate change adaptation.
Basic GIS operations include map overlay and buffering, which marks areas within a set distance of features such as roads or rivers.
Spatial interaction or gravity models estimate flows of people, materials or information between places.
Its most fundamental problem is how to define where the things being studied are located.
The ecological fallacy is the error of drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.
Land surveying, an early root of spatial analysis, goes back to at least 1,400 BC in Egypt, where taxable plots were measured with ropes.

definition.text: The tendency for values at nearby locations to be related to one another, either positively or negatively.

facts.text: It breaks the independence that standard statistics assume, so regressions that ignore it can give unstable estimates and unreliable significance tests.
Spatial regression models capture it, and it can also be seen as useful information rather than a nuisance.
Classic measures include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

definition.text: A source of statistical bias that arises because results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions.

facts.text: Summary values like totals, rates and densities depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.
A population density map built on state boundaries gives radically different results from one built on county boundaries.

definition.text: Using ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time.

facts.text: It can project a species' future range under climate change, its past range, or where an invasive species might spread.
A primary use is conservation: finding highly suitable habitat to prioritise sites for protection and restoration and guide protected area networks.
It helps identify climate refugia, places likely to stay suitable as the climate changes.
Correlative models fit a species' observed range to environmental conditions; mechanistic models use its physiology to work out where it could survive.
Correlative models are quicker but describe the realized niche and extrapolate poorly; mechanistic models handle shifting ranges better but need much physiological data.
MaxEnt is the most widely used method, working from presence-only records even when few are available.
Remote sensing and GIS-based environmental modelling greatly increased the data available for building these models.

definition.text: An approach to understanding how complex systems behave over time by modelling their stocks, flows, feedback loops and time delays.

facts.text: A stock is anything that builds up or runs down over time, and a flow is its rate of change.
The structure of a system, its circular, interlocking and delayed relationships, often matters as much as its individual parts.
Jay Forrester of MIT created it in the mid-1950s after showing by hand simulation that GE's employment swings came from the firm's own structure, not the business cycle.
Its best-known model is probably The Limits to Growth of 1972, which forecast economic collapse in the 21st century under many growth scenarios.
Models update all variables in small time steps, so mutual causation is handled through feedbacks and delays.
Typical applications are population, agricultural, ecological and economic systems, which interact strongly.
System dynamics and GIS are used together in spatial dynamic landscape simulation modelling in ecological economics.

definition.text: A simple map of a system's parts and how they affect each other, drawn to reveal its feedback loops.

facts.text: Reinforcing loops amplify change, as when more adopters of a product create stronger word of mouth; counteracting loops push back.
It supports qualitative analysis; for numbers it is turned into a stock and flow diagram and simulated on a computer.
Double slashes on an arrow mark a significant delay between cause and effect.

title: InVEST model

definition.text: InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs) is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services.

facts.text: It includes 20+ ecosystem service models covering land, freshwater, marine, coastal and urban settings.
It is used in more than 185 countries to map valuable ecological resources, weigh trade-offs in land and water use, and steer investments toward both conservation and development.
It is one of several tools, alongside the ARIES project and the Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, that help the private sector value ecosystem services.
Its developer works with governments, banks, companies and communities to bring nature's values into decisions through mapping, modelling and quantifying its benefits.
